feedback: If a learner says carbon is 'used up' or disappears once in the tree, point them back to following the same atom all the way around and ask them to name a route back to the air (respiration, combustion, decomposition).

If a learner thinks rising CO₂ means carbon is newly appearing, contrast the steady meter under natural processes with the climbing meter once fossil fuels/deforestation are switched on: the carbon was already stored, and is now moved rapidly into the air.
If a learner believes plants only release oxygen, highlight that plants also respire and return CO₂, so photosynthesis and respiration are the two balancing biological fluxes.
Confirm correct reasoning when a learner links the climbing meter to additions outpacing removals and can use the levers to slow the rise.
activities.intendedInsight: Carbon is conserved and recirculated through reservoirs (atmosphere, living things, fossil fuels); the climate problem is not that carbon moves but that humans add it to the air faster than natural processes (mainly photosynthesis in this model) remove it, tipping a budget that was roughly balanced before.
learnerActions: Trace a single carbon atom along its journey: drawn out of the air into a leaf by photosynthesis, eaten along a food chain (feeding), and breathed back out as CO₂ by respiration. Then follow it on a second trip: taken up again by a tree's photosynthesis, locked into wood that dies and is buried before decomposers can fully break it down, slowly turned into coal over millions of years (fossilisation), and finally released as CO₂ when the coal is burned (combustion). Note that if the dead wood had decomposed instead, the decomposers' respiration would have returned the carbon to the air much sooner.
Watch an atmospheric-CO₂ meter while only natural processes run, and state whether removal and return are roughly in balance.
Switch on fossil-fuel burning and deforestation, observe what the meter does, and write down what is actually changing (the rate of addition versus removal, not carbon appearing from nowhere).
Try to steady the meter by dialling emissions down and replanting forests, then explain what each lever does to the budget (replanting restores removal; cutting emissions reduces addition).

Tag each process with whether it ADDS atmospheric CO₂ (respiration, decomposition, combustion), REMOVES it (photosynthesis), or only moves carbon between stores without directly changing atmospheric CO₂ (feeding, fossilisation), and sort them into these groups.
activities.title: Follow one carbon atom and watch the CO₂ budget

feedback: For a 'why is CO₂ rising?' answer that says carbon is being created, redirect to conservation: the carbon was stored in fossil fuels and is now released faster than photosynthesis removes it.
For miscategorised processes, ask the learner which way the arrow points on the diagram they built.
Note that correctly closing the loop (naming all return routes) is required for a full response, not just labelling photosynthesis.
activities.intendedInsight: Pupils can confirm the model and, crucially, articulate the flux-balance reason for rising CO₂ rather than reciting that carbon 'increases'.
learnerActions: Categorise each process as adds-CO₂, removes-CO₂, or neither (moves carbon between other stores, e.g. feeding).
Sequence a carbon atom's path through the processes.
Match each process to the reservoir it moves carbon between.
Answer 'why is atmospheric CO₂ rising?' and justify the answer in terms of additions outpacing removals, not carbon being created.
activities.title: Check adds-vs-removes reasoning and why CO₂ is rising

feedback: If the learner attributes the tree's mass to soil (the van Helmont error), reteach photosynthesis as building matter from CO₂ and water; soil supplies only small amounts of mineral nutrients, not the bulk mass.
If the learner denies plants respire, establish that plants respire continuously as well as photosynthesising, releasing CO₂; use the aerobic respiration equation to make the return path concrete.
If the learner can name only 'plants take in CO₂' and no return routes, close the loop by naming respiration, combustion and decomposition as returns and stressing conservation.
Credit a full answer that traces atmospheric origin, names all return routes, states conservation, and explains fossil-fuel carbon and human disruption.
activities.intendedInsight: Full mastery: the tree's carbon came from atmospheric CO₂ via photosynthesis, returns via respiration (including the plant's own), combustion and decomposition, carbon is conserved, and human disruption is a change of rate that tips a balanced budget.
learnerActions: Respond to the diagnostic: 'A giant oak tree weighs several tonnes. Where did most of that material — the wood, and the carbon in it — actually come from: the soil, or somewhere else? Explain how the carbon got into the tree, and then how that same carbon can end up back in the air.'

Answer probing follow-ups: Van Helmont grew a willow for five years; it gained about 74 kg while the soil lost only about 57 g — where did the extra mass come from? Do plants respire as well as photosynthesise, and what does that mean for carbon? Coal is 'buried sunshine' — trace its carbon back to where it first came from. Name three different ways the carbon locked in that oak could return to the atmosphere.

State explicitly what has changed under human activity: not that carbon moves at all, but that burning fossil fuels unlocks long-stored carbon into the air, while deforestation removes the forests that would take CO₂ back — so additions now outpace removals.
activities.title: Explain: carbon has always cycled — so what changed?
